name: Iris Novak

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Iris. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any AI company, employer, union, party or government, and we're not selling anything. Everything you tell me stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I drill blast holes at an open-pit nickel mine, on a rotary drill rig about forty tonnes. The surveyors mark the pattern, I line the rig up on each spot, drill down about fifteen metres, pull out, move to the next. Maybe forty holes a shift if the ground's kind. I like that it's just me and the machine and the hum, nobody talking at me. What wears me out is the cold in winter mornings when the hydraulics are slow and so am I.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: You said nobody talking at you. Is that why you chose drilling?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Partly. I came from a farm, I like quiet work you can see the end of. Marek, my husband, was an electrician, he's retired now and fixes everyone's toasters. Our son Tomas works on ships overseas and our daughter Ana's an accountant in town. We've got a little cabin by the lake and a good bit put by. I've got a phone for calls and pictures of the grandchildren, that's all I use it for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: I'm going to read you five pictures of the future, one at a time. The first is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say well, that's that then. I'm not one for saying much at work and I don't go online. If someone on the break brought it up, I'd shrug.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think AI Plateau means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I drill until sixty-three, like I planned, and then I go to the lake. I've never used one of these AI things and I'm not about to start. So it was never really about me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing. I'd keep drilling and keep putting money aside. I might take Marek to see Tomas in the spring, we keep saying we will.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Same as I feel about the weather forecast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you hear much talk about AI at the mine?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only from the young ones. They talk about the drills at the other site that run on their own, with someone watching from an office. That's not AI to me, that's just a fancy drill, but I suppose it's the same thing in the end.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the next few years look like for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years of holes, then the cabin. Marek wants a boat, I want a vegetable garden. We'll probably have both.

S0.say: I'd say well, that's that then. I don't say much at work and I don't go online, so I'd just shrug if it came up.
S0.think: She believes it means drilling until sixty-three as planned, then retiring to the lake. She's never used AI tools and doesn't intend to, so it was never really about her.
S0.do: Keeps drilling and keeps putting money aside with no change. Plans a spring trip with Marek to visit their son overseas.
S0.feel: Calm, like listening to the weather forecast.
S0.quote: Same as I feel about the weather forecast.
S0.fieldNote: Iris is dry and few-worded, a farm kid who likes quiet work she can see the end of. She doesn't connect AI with the self-driving drills at the other site until she talks it through. Her cushion is solid with savings and a lake cabin.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's business, the company's got to make money like anyone else. I wouldn't make a fuss. But I'd say they should look after the people who've given them twenty years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think Steady Disruption means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think they'd bring one of those self-driving rigs in and I'd be the one told to watch it. I don't want to sit in an office staring at screens. I'd rather leave than do that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait and see what the company offers before doing anything. I'd put a bit more into savings, maybe hold off on the new car. If they offered me a package at sixty, I'd probably take it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, quietly. Like when you hear a noise in the engine and you're not sure if it's anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the drills at the other site that run on their own. What if one came to your pit?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask to stay on the old rig as long as there is one. Some jobs always need a person, the odd holes, the bad ground. If not, I'd go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you think would be responsible for looking after people like you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The company first, because they're the ones saving the money. Then the government, a bit. Not the union, I'm a member but I don't expect much from them, they're good at meetings.

S1.say: I'd say it's business and the company has to make money like anyone else. I wouldn't make a fuss, but they should look after people who've given them twenty years.
S1.think: She thinks they'd bring in a self-driving rig and ask her to watch it from an office, which she doesn't want. She'd rather leave than stare at screens.
S1.do: Waits to see what the company offers before acting, and puts a bit more into savings while holding off on a new car. Would take a package at sixty if offered.
S1.feel: Quietly uneasy, like hearing a noise in the engine and not knowing if it's anything.
S1.quote: I don't want to sit in an office staring at screens. I'd rather leave than do that.
S1.fieldNote: She doesn't blame anyone loudly; she treats automation as ordinary business. Her line in the sand is screen work, which she'd rather leave than do. She is a union member with low expectations of the union.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's too fast, nobody can get ready in two years. The government needs to make sure older workers aren't just dumped. Not handouts, a fair package, that's all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think AGI by 2028 means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I'm finished at sixty, three years early. We've got enough to get by, with the savings and Marek's pension, but it'd be tighter than we wanted. And I don't know what I'd do with myself all day, I'm not a sit-still person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First thing, I'd ask Ana to go through our money with me, she's the accountant. Then I'd stop spending on anything big, no new car, no boat for Marek. And I'd take whatever package they offered, rather than wait to be pushed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Like being told the harvest's coming two weeks early and the barn's not ready.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd be sixty when this arrives. How does that sit with the plan for sixty-three?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sixty is three years earlier than I planned. Ana would know the numbers, I don't keep them in my head. I know we'd be all right, but all right isn't what we saved for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut first, if you needed to?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The boat. Marek would sulk, but it's the boat. Then the trip to see Tomas, maybe, which would hurt more.

S2.say: I'd say that's too fast, nobody can get ready in two years. The government should make sure older workers aren't just dumped, with a fair package rather than handouts.
S2.think: She expects to be finished at sixty, three years early, with enough to get by on savings and Marek's pension but tighter than planned. She doesn't know what she'd do with herself all day.
S2.do: Asks her daughter, an accountant, to go through their finances, and stops big spending, starting with the boat. Takes whatever package is offered rather than waiting to be pushed.
S2.feel: Anxious, like the harvest coming two weeks early with the barn not ready.
S2.quote: I know we'd be all right, but all right isn't what we saved for.
S2.fieldNote: Her farm background shapes her metaphors and her practicality. Money would hold, but the retirement she saved for would shrink. She leans on her daughter rather than any outside help, and wants a fair package, not handouts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough for the company to do it properly. Give people their packages and some notice. That's fair.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think AGI by 2031 means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years, I'm sixty-three. That's exactly when I meant to stop. So it's like it was planned for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep drilling and keep saving, and I'd tell my supervisor I'll go at sixty-three, no fuss. Maybe a bit more into savings in case they push me out earlier. Otherwise the same.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but only a little. It lines up with my own plans, mostly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How is five years different for you from two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years is being pushed off the truck. Five years, I get to climb down. That's the difference.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you think about learning to run the rig from an office, given five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I've thought about it and no. I'd rather finish on the rig or not at all.

S3.say: I'd say five years is enough for the company to do it properly, with packages and some notice. That's fair.
S3.think: Five years takes her to sixty-three, exactly when she meant to stop, so it feels almost planned for her. She worries only that she might be pushed out a bit earlier.
S3.do: Keeps drilling and tells her supervisor she'll leave at sixty-three without fuss. Puts a bit more into savings in case she's pushed out earlier.
S3.feel: Only a little uneasy, because it mostly lines up with her plans.
S3.quote: Two years is being pushed off the truck. Five years, I get to climb down.
S3.fieldNote: Five years matches her own retirement date almost exactly, which takes most of the sting out. She flatly refuses screen work even with time to learn. Her phrase about climbing down rather than being pushed captures what the time buys her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, people should get on with it. The ones who want to learn something new have time. I'd leave it at that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think AGI by 2036 means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It doesn't touch me. I'll be at the lake with my vegetables. The rigs can drive themselves for all I care by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as now. Drill to sixty-three, then go. Keep saving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It's somebody else's future.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: By 2036 you'd be sixty-eight. Does this one touch you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ana says AI does half her accounting work already, so she worries more than me. Tomas, I don't know, ships are ships. I'd tell them to look after themselves and keep some money aside, like I did.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Anything about your children or grandchildren in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd miss the rig, I suppose. Not the cold. The hum.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is plenty and people should get on with it. Those who want to learn something new have time.
S4.think: It doesn't touch her, because she'll be retired at the lake with her vegetables. The rigs can drive themselves by then for all she cares.
S4.do: Carries on drilling until sixty-three as planned and keeps saving each month. Makes no other changes and leaves the new technology to younger workers.
S4.feel: Calm, because it feels like somebody else's future.
S4.quote: I'd miss the rig, I suppose. Not the cold. The hum.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years she simply steps aside, and the change happens after her working life. The only feeling she lets slip is missing the hum of the rig. She notes her accountant daughter is more worried than she is.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because it would take three years off my working life without asking. What would help is a fair package for people near the end, so we can go with dignity. And some notice, that's all.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: No. You asked plenty. Maybe ask the young ones more, they've got further to go.

headlineQuote: That's not AI to me, that's just a fancy drill, but I suppose it's the same thing in the end.
portrait: Iris Novak is a 58-year-old blast hole drill operator at an open-pit nickel mine, a quiet former farm kid who likes the hum of her rig and never uses AI. She and her retired electrician husband have good savings and a lake cabin. She treats automation as ordinary business and refuses to move into screen work. Only the two-year AGI picture really worries her, because it would cut three years off her working life and shrink the retirement they saved for. With five or ten years she lines the change up with her own plan to retire at sixty-three.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because it would take three years off her working life without asking.
whatWouldHelp: A fair package for people near the end of their working lives so they can go with dignity, and some notice.
